lead: An inertial navigation system carries its own sensors and asks nothing of the outside world. Three accelerometers measure the push needed to hold a proof mass still, three gyros measure how fast the aircraft turns, and a computer integrates these to give velocity and position. Nothing is transmitted, so nothing can be jammed. The catch is drift: small sensor biases integrate into position errors that grow with time. INS is usually blended with GPS (see Kalman filter and GPS-INS integration).
prereq: You need gyroscopes for gyro behaviour, geometric concepts of navigation for the frames, and the accelerometer in Aircraft transducers: solenoids, pressure, temperature, strain, rotary position and accelerometers.

sections.h3: Accelerometers measure specific force, gyros measure rate

blocks.text: An accelerometer holds a small proof mass. When the case accelerates the mass lags; a strain gauge, capacitor or piezoelectric crystal senses the displacement. A force-rebalance accelerometer pushes the mass back to null with a coil and outputs the coil current, keeping the sensor linear and stiff.

The output is specific force f, not acceleration in space. At rest the accelerometer reads 1 g upward: the ground pushes the mass up. In free fall it reads zero, though it accelerates at 9.81 m/s². To get inertial acceleration, add gravity back.

blocks.where: a is inertial acceleration (m/s²); f is measured specific force (m/s²); g is gravitational acceleration (m/s²), 9.81 m/s² downward. At rest f is 9.81 m/s² upward, so a = 0.

blocks.text: Gyros are rate sensors. A ring laser gyro sends two beams round a triangular cavity in opposite directions; rotation makes their path lengths differ, and the beat frequency is proportional to rate (the Sagnac effect). A fibre-optic gyro does the same in a coil of fibre with no moving parts. MEMS gyros shake a tiny mass and read the Coriolis force. Output is angular rate ω in °/s or °/h; one integration gives angle.

Bias is the output at zero input; scale factor error is the slope error, in ppm or %. Gyro bias is quoted in °/h and accelerometer bias in mg, where 1 mg = 0.00981 m/s² and 1 µg = 9.81 × 10⁻⁶ m/s² (one millionth of a g).

sections.h3: Frames, mechanizations and the inertial chain

blocks.text: Besides the inertial, ECEF and NED frames, the INS uses the body frame bolted to the airframe: x forward, y right, z down. Vectors move between frames by a direction cosine matrix (DCM, a 3×3 matrix of direction cosines), or by a quaternion — four numbers with no singularity at 90° pitch. Attitude is the DCM from body to NED.

Two mechanizations exist. In a gimballed system the sensors sit on a platform that torque motors hold level and pointing north while the aircraft turns around it, so the sensors see almost no rotation. In a strapdown system the sensors are bolted to the airframe and see the full rotation rate, so the computer carries attitude continuously. Strapdown won — smaller, cheaper, more reliable — at the cost of computing power and a wider sensor range.

items: Gyros give body rates ω; integrate them with the DCM to update body-to-NED attitude.
Accelerometers give f in body axes; rotate f into NED with that same DCM.
Add gravity: a = f + g, where g points down (third component +g in NED).
Integrate a once for velocity, then again for position.
Feed position back to the attitude step so the local level follows the Earth's curvature.

sections.h3: Alignment, Schuler tuning and error growth

blocks.text: Before use the INS must be aligned: its starting attitude must be found. Levelling uses the accelerometers — any tilt puts a horizontal component of gravity into f, so the pitch and roll that null it are correct. Gyrocompassing uses the gyros: the Earth turns at 15.04 °/h and its horizontal component points north. The heading at which the east-pointing gyro senses no Earth rate is north, found with no magnetic reference. Alignment needs a few minutes and the aircraft still.

A feedback from position to attitude is tuned to the Schuler period. A level platform carried over a round Earth behaves like a pendulum of length equal to the Earth's radius. Tuned to that natural period, a horizontal acceleration produces no steady tilt: the platform swings instead of drifting off level as the aircraft crosses the curved Earth.

blocks.where: T is the Schuler period (s); R = 6.371 × 10⁶ m is the Earth's radius; g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: Errors after alignment grow by integration. In the first few minutes (well under 84.4 min ÷ 2π ≈ 13 min) the Schuler loop has not yet acted, and the open-loop forms hold: an accelerometer bias b gives velocity error bt and position error ½bt²; a gyro bias ε tilts the platform by εt, giving a false horizontal acceleration gεt, velocity error ½gεt² and position error gεt³/6.

blocks.where: Δp is position error (m); b is accelerometer bias (m/s²); ε is gyro bias (rad/s); t is time since alignment (s); g = 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: Over longer times the Schuler loop bounds the tilt. An accelerometer bias then gives a position error that oscillates with the 84.4 min period instead of growing as ½bt². A gyro bias still gives a position error that grows, but as a ramp with an 84.4 min ripple, not as t³:
Δp = R ε (t − sin(ω<sub>s</sub>t) ÷ ω<sub>s</sub>),   ω<sub>s</sub> = √(g ÷ R)
blocks.where: Δp is the position error with the Schuler loop closed (m); R = 6.371 × 10⁶ m; ε is the gyro bias (rad/s); ω<sub>s</sub> = 1.241 × 10⁻³ rad/s is the Schuler frequency. For small t this reduces to gεt³/6; for long t it grows as Rεt.

blocks.text: So a gyro bias of 0.01 °/h costs about Rε = 0.31 m/s, roughly 0.6 nm every hour: the "nautical mile per hour" class of a navigation-grade INS. Gyro quality sets the long-term accuracy. The cure is an outside fix blended in by a Kalman filter (see Kalman filter and GPS-INS integration).

figure.caption: Top, the strapdown chain with its Schuler feedback. Bottom, the worked example's 0.01 °/h gyro bias: the open-loop t³ curve (dashed) holds only for minutes; with the Schuler loop the error is 1.35 km at one hour.

spec.aria: Top, five blocks in a row: IMU, attitude integration, resolving specific force into north-east-down, adding gravity, and integrating twice to velocity and position, with a dashed Schuler feedback loop from position back to attitude. Bottom, a graph of position error in kilometres against time in hours for a 0.01 degree per hour gyro bias: the dashed open-loop cubic curve reaches 3.70 kilometres at one hour, while the solid Schuler-loop curve is 1.35 kilometres at one hour and rises as a gentle ramp with a ripple to about 3.2 kilometres at three hours.

examples.question: An inertial system is aligned and then runs unaided. (a) An accelerometer bias of 1 mg acts along a horizontal axis: find the velocity and position errors after 100 s. (b) A gyro bias of 0.01 °/h acts about a level axis: find the position error after 10 minutes from the open-loop formula, and after one hour with the Schuler loop closed. Take g = 9.81 m/s² and R = 6.371 × 10⁶ m.
steps: (a) Position error = ½bt² = 0.5 × 9.81 × 10⁻³ × 100² = 49.05 m. 100 s is far below 13 min, so the open-loop form is right.
(b) After 10 min (t = 600 s): Δp = gεt³/6 = 9.81 × 4.848 × 10⁻⁸ × 600³ ÷ 6 = 17.1 m. (The Schuler formula gives 16.7 m: at 10 min the two still agree.)
Compare: the open-loop gεt³/6 at 1 h would give 3698 m, almost three times too much, because it ignores the Schuler loop that stops the tilt growing.
examples.answer: (a) 0.981 m/s and 49.05 m after 100 s. (b) about 17 m after 10 min, and about 1.35 km after 1 h with the Schuler loop closed (the open-loop formula would wrongly give 3.7 km).

traps: An accelerometer at rest reads 1 g, not zero — it senses specific force. Writing a = f and forgetting gravity loses marks.
Convert units first: 1 °/h = 4.848 × 10⁻⁶ rad/s, 1 mg = 0.00981 m/s². And use gεt³/6 only for the first few minutes; over an hour it overstates the error.
Gyrocompassing senses Earth's rotation of 15.04 °/h, not magnetic north, so magnetic variation never enters alignment.

quiz.q: What does an accelerometer in an INS actually measure?
quiz.a: Specific force — the non-gravitational push per unit mass. It reads 9.81 m/s² upward at rest and zero in free fall; add gravity back to get acceleration in space.

quiz.q: Why does a strapdown system demand more computation than a gimballed one?
quiz.a: Its sensors are bolted to the airframe and see the full rotation rate, so attitude must be integrated continuously in software. Gimbals stabilise physically, so the sensors see almost no rotation.

quiz.q: Why is the inertial loop tuned to the 84.4 min Schuler period?
quiz.a: So the platform behaves like a pendulum of length equal to the Earth's radius. A horizontal acceleration then causes no steady tilt; the platform oscillates about level instead of drifting off it as the aircraft crosses the curved Earth.

quiz.q: A gyro bias of 0.05 °/h is left uncorrected for 5 minutes. Find the position error using gεt³/6, and say why the formula may be used.
quiz.a: ε = 0.05 × 4.848 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.424 × 10⁻⁷ rad/s; t = 300 s. Δp = 9.81 × 2.424 × 10⁻⁷ × 300³ ÷ 6 = 10.7 m. Five minutes is well below 13 min, so the Schuler loop has not yet acted and the open-loop form holds.

quiz.q: In the first few minutes, why does a gyro bias give a position error growing as t³ while an accelerometer bias gives t²?
quiz.a: The gyro bias first tilts the platform by εt; the tilt turns gravity into a false horizontal acceleration gεt, which is integrated twice for position. A constant accelerometer bias is already an acceleration and needs only two integrations.

quiz.q: Gyrocompassing is easy near the equator and hard near the poles. Explain.
quiz.a: Ω = 15.04 °/h is the Earth's rotation rate and φ is the latitude, so the sensed horizontal Earth rate is Ω cos φ. This falls to zero at the pole while gyro bias stays fixed; the signal-to-noise ratio collapses, so alignment takes longer and eventually fails.

beyond: Not for the exam. Airliners fly strapdown units on ring laser or fibre-optic gyros; MEMS units of the same design sit in phones and drones. Cold-atom sensors are a research direction. Search 'ring laser gyro dither', 'Sagnac effect fibre gyro' and 'transfer alignment'.
